newsitem.title: UK: IRA's brogue-accent baffled British spies of 1920s.
newsitem.headline: IRA's brogue-accent baffled British spies of 1920s.

text.p: Britain tried to infiltrate the nascent Irish Republican Army (IRA) early this century but newly-released documents show that secret agents were baffled by brogue, the rebels" thick accent.
The James Bonds of that era used microphones in a high-tech surveillance scheme but were spooked by the Irish accent.
According to public records British spies bugged Irish republican leaders, including Michael Collins whose life is the subject of a controversial new film which opens in London and Dublin next week.
But they could barely understand a word.
"Microphones of English manufacture seem ill-adapted to the Irish brogue," wrote Major Ormond Winter, Britain's head of intelligence in Ireland in a 1921 report.

The records, dating from between 1853 and the early 1920s, are among the oldest to have been kept secret, reflecting the continuing sensitivity over Northern Ireland. Most records are released after either 30 or 50 years.

They reveal that Irish informants were paid up to 200 pounds ($325) a year, equivalent to about 60,000 pounds today, but their information proved of little value because the republican movement's own intelligence was so effective.
The IRA and its political wing Sinn Fein were able to listen into telephone conversations by the British military because they had effective control over the Irish telephone system, the records said.
The papers cover one of the most fraught periods in Anglo-Irish history after the 1916 Dublin Uprising by Irish nationalists against British rule.
Three years of bloodshed between the IRA and British irregular forces followed before Ireland was partitioned with separate parliaments in Belfast and Dublin.
Winter wrote that another problem for the British agents was their inability to understand the Irish psyche.
"It has been said that no European can fathom the mind of an Oriental and it might equally be said that no Englishman can fully grasp the inner psychology of the Irish rebel character."
To make complicate matters further, "there are no means of distinguishing the potential spy from any other Irish man," Winter said.
